title: Has the pendulum swung too far away from "college for all"?
author: Mike Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli, who has himself championed the shift toward CTE pathways and away from 'college for all' messaging, uses this piece to question whether that pendulum has swung too far, particularly for strong first-generation and lower-income students who could thrive at selective four-year institutions but are now hearing from every direction that college may not be worth it. He argues the underlying earnings and mobility data for selective four-year degrees, especially in fields with labor market demand, remain strong and haven't changed, but that the cultural permission structure around choosing that path has shifted, especially for kids without family precedent for college. Central to his argument is a distinction between a well-off kid opting out of college from a position of security versus a talented, low-income kid being nudged away from the option with the best odds of changing their family's trajectory. Rather than swinging back to a universal college-for-all message, he calls for the return of genuinely individualized counseling that matches a specific kid's interests, numbers, and family situation to the best path for them, rather than any one-size-fits-all default in either direction.
points: Written by an author who has himself promoted the shift toward CTE and trades messaging, making this a self-critical reconsideration rather than an outside attack on that consensus.

Distinguishes between a well-off kid opting out of college from a position of security and a talented, low-income first-generation kid being nudged away from the option with the best odds of changing their family's trajectory.

Argues the underlying earnings and mobility data for selective four-year degrees, especially in labor-market-relevant fields, remain strong and unchanged, even as the cultural permission structure around choosing college has shifted.

Rejects returning to a universal 'college for all' message and instead calls for genuinely individualized, hard-to-scale counseling matched to a specific student's interests, numbers, and family situation.
quotes: But lately I've started to wonder whether we're overcorrecting, and whether the new consensus is quietly doing damage to a group of kids who don't fit either the old or the new story.

The data on selective four-year degrees, particularly in fields with real labor market demand, remain very strong. That has not changed. What has changed is the cultural permission structure around choosing that path.

A kid from a highly educated family who decides to skip college and become an electrician is making a choice from a position of security; college was always available to them, and they are opting out of it.
They are being nudged out of the option that had the best odds of changing their family's trajectory, potentially without ever being told clearly what the earnings data actually show.

But the current mood risks creating a new one-size-fits-all default, just pointed in the opposite direction, and it will do the most damage to exactly the kids who have the least other information to draw on.

It's the return of genuinely individualized guidance, the unglamorous, expensive, hard-to-scale work of a counselor or mentor who knows a specific kid well enough to say, for you, specifically... here is the path that gives you the best shot.
